In this report, CHIJIOKE IREMEKA reports that despite Nigeria’s restrictions on certain agrochemicals, some of the products remain available in open markets and are sold to households for indoor pest control In Ibusa, Delta State, 31-year-old Patience Okorie and her five-month-old baby experienced health problems after she used an insecticide known as DD Force to fumigate her home against mosquitoes, cockroaches and other household pests. Okorie said she and her baby subsequently experienced respiratory symptoms and were diagnosed with acute toxicity at a general hospital. Their experience highlights the potential health risks associated with the misuse of agricultural chemicals, particularly when products intended for crop protection are used in residential environments. Insecticides, often relied upon for pest control, can pose serious health risks when used improperly or without observing the necessary safety precautions. According to the National Agency for Food and Drug Administration and Control, the sale of small-volume dichlorvos formulations (100ml or less), sold under brands such as Sniper and DD Force, among others, has been prohibited since 2019. The sale of larger volumes is subject to restrictions, including distribution through accredited agrochemical outlets. “NAFDAC bans the importation and manufacture of 100ml pack size of Agricultural formulations of Dichlorvos with immediate effect. NAFDAC bans, with immediate effect, the hawking of all agrochemical formulations. “NAFDAC is giving a two-month (up to 31st August 2019) notice to brand owners/distributors to recall and withdraw their products from open markets and supermarkets that do not have garden corner/shelves to the agro dealer outlets. “The sales of Sniper insecticide and other Dichlorvos brands in open markets and supermarkets nationwide are prohibited with effect from 1st September 2019. NAFDAC is giving a six-month moratorium up to 1st January 2020 for brand owners to exhaust the products that are in various accredited agro-input dealers (distributors/marketers/retailers),” the agency stated. Banned but still in circulation Chemicals subject to bans include Aldrin Insecticide, Binapacryl, Captafol, Chlordane, Chlordimeform, DDT Insecticide, Dieldrin, Dinoseb and Dinoseb Salts, Heptachlor Herbicide, Lindane, Ethylene Dichloride, Parathion, Methyl Parathion, Phosphamidon and Monocrotophos. Others are Methamidophos, Chlorobenzilate, Toxaphene, Pentachlorophenol Herbicide, Ethylene Oxide Fumigant, HCF (Mixed Isomers), EDB (1,2-Dibromoethene), 2,4,5-Trichlorophenoxy Acetic Acid, Endrin, Mirex, Ethylene Dibromide, Hexachlorobenzene, Endosulphan Acaricide, Delta HCH Agricultural and Fluoroacetamide. An investigation by Saturday PUNCH found that some products containing dichlorvos, including brands such as NOPEST, DD Force and Sniper, were still being sold in open markets, food markets and provision stalls. NAFDAC has warned that certain pesticides contain organophosphates and other toxic substances that can cause respiratory disorders, skin irritation and neurological problems, among other health effects. Insecticide use linked to health problems The nursing mother, Okorie, said she had given birth without complications in February 2025 and had been living well with her baby while keeping regular immunisation appointments until the child was diagnosed with malaria at a community health centre. Following the diagnosis, she decided to purchase a small bottle of DD Force to control mosquitoes in her home. She said the product had been recommended to her because of its perceived effectiveness against mosquitoes and cockroaches. Saturday PUNCH learnt that DD Force is an agricultural insecticide used to control a wide range of crop pests, including beetles, caterpillars, mealybugs, grasshoppers and locusts. Its product labelling also carries warnings about its potential hazards. The mother, who occasionally used Sniper before purchasing DD Force, said she bought the product at Eke Market and used it to fumigate her home. “After using this DD Force, I first noticed that the smell was still very strong and harsh even several hours after use. I used it mainly when everybody had gone out, especially on Sundays. “I noticed how strong the chemical was. Even while spraying it, it made you cough repeatedly the moment you inhaled it. Even after spraying it, I would still cough for some minutes. “Ignorantly, I felt it was strong enough to achieve my desire, not knowing it was affecting our health. Even five hours later, the smell would still be strong in the house despite opening the windows to allow for cross-ventilation,” she said. According to her, the coughing continued until she became concerned about her persistent symptoms and those of her baby. She also observed that their breathing had become noisy before they visited Ibusa General Hospital. “At first, they suspected asthma at the health centre where we visited due to the wheezing cough, but I told them that I had never suffered from it, nor had anybody in my family. So, we were referred to the General Hospital. “After answering a series of questions from the doctor and undergoing medical tests, it was discovered that our condition was caused by the insecticide I was using,” she explained. Okorie said she and her baby experienced persistent coughing, shortness of breath and chest tightness. She said the symptoms became more noticeable following the use of the product, prompting her to seek medical attention. According to her account, the attending physician explained that exposure to the insecticide had triggered an inflammatory response in her lungs, worsening her breathing difficulties. She said the physician advised her to discontinue its use and commenced treatment to manage the symptoms. The experience was physically and emotionally distressing for the mother, who was particularly worried about her baby’s condition. While receiving treatment, she said she was advised to leave the house for three days to allow it to air out. She told our correspondent that she stayed at her parents’ house in Ogbo-Owere and returned after four days. Her husband had also spent four days at a camp in Ogwasi-Ukwu. “I was advised to net my home instead of using an indoor residual spray. I was told that spraying would only be necessary as an alternative mosquito-control strategy,” she said. ‘I had to undergo detoxification’ Similarly, a 26-year-old factory worker, who lives in Ejigbo, Lagos State, said he experienced persistent headaches accompanied by dizziness, irritability, nausea and fatigue after regularly using Sniper in his apartment. He said he had relied on pesticides to control mosquitoes, ants and termites that occasionally damaged the wooden frames of his doors. “I usually make use of a particular insecticide until it proves ineffective. I rented a room-and-parlour apartment in Ejigbo, Lagos, a few months ago and needed to fumigate the room against cockroaches, mosquitoes, ants and other creeping things. “I didn’t have money for a total fumigation, which would cost me N40,000. So, I sought something stronger and cheaper. I bought a big container of it. I started using Sniper then, and I have been doing so for over eight months. Of course, I wasn’t having any problems with cockroaches and mosquitoes, as I also netted my house,” he said. The factory worker said he sometimes returned home late, diluted the insecticide with water and sprayed it around his apartment. He admitted that on several occasions, he went to sleep in the room even when the chemical had not completely evaporated because he was tired. He said he subsequently began experiencing persistent headaches, dizziness and nausea. Make PUNCH part of your everyday experience. Concerned about the symptoms, he visited a family physician, who, according to him, conducted tests and identified elevated levels of toxins in his body, which the physician linked to his insecticide exposure. “I underwent serious treatment and a detoxification process involving medications to counteract the toxic effects. I had persistent migraines and underwent extensive therapy to manage the illness,” he added. An outdoor chemical used indoors Findings revealed that Sniper, like other agricultural insecticides containing dichlorvos, also known as DDVP, is primarily intended for agricultural pest control but is sometimes used in homes. Saturday PUNCH’s checks revealed that Sniper is marketed by an international agrochemical company with operations in several countries. According to the manufacturer’s website, “Sniper is a highly effective insecticide/miticide that controls over 30 foliar and soil-borne pests, which gives growers the flexibility and residual activity needed to combat insects in conventional or biotech systems.” The website also describes the product as a restricted-use pesticide. According to a product brochure, the insecticide is “toxic to fish and aquatic organisms” and “may be fatal if swallowed”. Under its precautionary statements, the product is described as a “hazard to humans and domestic animals”. Further warnings indicate that it is “harmful if inhaled or absorbed through the skin” and advise users to “avoid breathing vapour or spray mist”. NAFDAC has warned that certain chemicals used in pesticides have been prohibited in Nigeria and other countries because of their potential health and environmental effects. The agency has emphasised that exposure to some of these substances can have short-term and long-term consequences. In a 2019 statement titled, ‘NAFDAC Warns Nigerians Against Use of Dichlorvos Chemical for Food Preservation, Says It Can Cause Cancer, Death,’ the agency stated: “Long-term exposure can result in severe health implications, including developmental abnormalities in offspring, memory loss, reduced fertility, and potential carcinogenic effects. “These adverse effects highlight the importance of adhering to safety guidelines to mitigate the risks associated with dichlorvos exposure,” it said. NAFDAC also raised concerns about the importation and use of pesticides prohibited in Europe, citing a study by the Heinrich Böll Foundation which stated that 40 per cent of pesticides used in Nigeria had been banned in the European Union. On July 12, 2019, the agency issued a statement announcing restrictions on a range of agrochemicals, including 100ml packs of Sniper insecticide, NOPEST and DD Force. Other affected brands included 100ml packs of agricultural dichlorvos formulations such as Tankill, Gladiator Liquid, Executor Liquid, Smash Super Liquid, Glovan, Philopest, Wonder Liquid, Rid-Off and SUMODDVP. NAFDAC cited product misuse as household insecticides, suicide and direct misapplication on agricultural produce among the reasons for the restrictions. It also identified serious public-health concerns, including cancer and respiratory disorders. The agency stated that DD Force and other dichlorvos formulations were agricultural insecticides registered for use as crop-protection products. “NAFDAC bans the importation and manufacture of 100ml pack sizes of agricultural formulations of dichlorvos with immediate effect. “NAFDAC bans with immediate effect the hawking of all agrochemical formulations. The sale of DD Force, Sniper insecticide and other dichlorvos brands in open markets and supermarkets nationwide is prohibited with effect from September 1, 2019,” the agency stated. ‘Can result in acute poisoning’ According to the World Health Organisation, more than 1,000 pesticides are used around the world to protect food from damage or destruction by pests, and each pesticide has different properties and toxicological effects. The global health body stated that some older, less costly pesticides, such as dichlorodiphenyltrichloroethane and lindane, can remain in soil and water for years. It noted that some of these chemicals have been prohibited by countries that signed the 2001 Stockholm Convention, an international treaty aimed at eliminating or restricting the production and use of persistent organic pollutants. “The toxicity of a pesticide depends on its function and other factors. For example, insecticides tend to be more toxic to humans than herbicides. The same chemical can have different effects at different doses, that is, the amount of chemical to which a person is exposed. TB killed 1.1 million people globally in 2025 — WHO US, Nasarawa spend N7bn on 1.8m mosquito nets Delta targets 5,000 jobs from glass factory revival “Toxicity can also depend on the route by which the exposure occurs, such as by swallowing, inhaling or direct contact with the skin. None of the pesticides currently authorised for use on food in international trade are genotoxic (damaging to DNA, which can cause mutations or cancer). “Adverse effects from these pesticides occur only above a certain safe level of exposure. When people come into contact with large quantities of pesticide, the result may be acute poisoning or long-term health effects that may include cancer and adverse effects on reproduction,” the WHO added. A consultant public health physician at the Federal Medical Centre, Asaba, Delta State, Dr Ovie Efekodo, said prohibited and improperly used insecticides could pose significant risks to human health and the environment. According to him, exposure to hazardous chemicals could result in serious health problems, disrupt ecosystems and impose substantial financial costs. He said addressing the risks required adherence to safety regulations, the use of safer alternatives and increased public awareness. Efekodo explained that some insecticides could cause respiratory disorders and acute poisoning, with symptoms including headaches, dizziness, nausea, vomiting and abdominal pain. Severe cases could result in seizures or loss of consciousness. He noted that acute poisoning could occur through inhalation, ingestion or absorption through the skin, adding that some insecticides affect the nervous system or interfere with essential physiological processes. A consultant pulmonologist and Head of the Respiratory Unit at the Obafemi Awolowo University Teaching Hospitals Complex, Ile-Ife, Prof Gregory Erhabor, said prolonged exposure to certain insecticides, including organophosphates, could contribute to chronic respiratory problems. The specialist in respiratory diseases and former president of the Nigerian Thoracic Society said possible effects included persistent coughing and other respiratory complications. Erhabor, who is also the president and founder of the Asthma and Chest Care Foundation, warned against exposure to and inhalation of harmful chemicals. “Some banned insecticides have been linked to an increased risk of various cancers, including leukaemia, lymphoma and breast cancer. Carcinogenic chemicals can cause cellular mutations that lead to cancerous growths,” he added. Reproductive health concerns A consultant gynaecologist and surgeon at the Federal Medical Centre, Epe, Lagos State, Dr Cynthia Okafor, warned that exposure to certain harmful insecticides could have implications for reproductive health. She said some chemicals had been associated with adverse outcomes during pregnancy and could affect foetal development. “Pregnant women exposed to banned insecticides may face risks of birth defects and developmental delays in their children. Chemicals like DDT have been associated with negative outcomes in foetal development. “Long-term exposure to certain chemicals can affect reproductive health, potentially leading to fertility issues or reproductive system disorders,” she added. The United States Environmental Protection Agency has also warned about the potential consequences of exposure to certain pesticides and restricted the use of a particular herbicide over concerns about its effects on foetal development. Known as dimethyl tetrachloroterephthalate, the herbicide is used to control weeds on several crops, including broccoli, onions, kale, Brussels sprouts, cabbage and strawberries. The EPA stated that exposure could cause changes in foetal thyroid hormone levels. “Low birth weight, impaired brain development, decreased IQ and impaired motor skills later in life are some of the consequences. “It’s EPA’s job to protect people from exposure to dangerous chemicals. In this case, pregnant women who may never even know they were exposed could give birth to babies that experience irreversible lifelong health problems,” the agency added. Products still sold in open markets Findings by Saturday PUNCH showed that some of the agrochemical products subject to regulatory restrictions remained available in open markets. During visits to several markets in Lagos State, our correspondent observed different insecticide products being displayed and sold by traders, including some of the restricted 100ml packs. Although larger pack sizes were also available, smaller packs were less frequently encountered. Other products with different brand names were also observed. The findings are consistent with NAFDAC’s recent concerns about the continued circulation of prohibited and unregistered pesticides in Nigeria. At Alaba International Market in Ojo, along St Peter’s Road, leading to Green Gate, Ilufe, our correspondent observed a cart pusher displaying different insecticides, including products labelled DDVP and DD Force, alongside rat poison and other household items. The practice of hawking agrochemical formulations is contrary to NAFDAC’s directive prohibiting the hawking of such products. A trader selling the products from a cart said he had operated in Alaba and Iyana-Iba for about two years without receiving any warning from regulatory officials. “I started this business in the last two years. I sell in Alaba and Iyana-Iba, but nobody has said anything to me. The only people who disturb me are the revenue collectors, not even NAFDAC,” he told our correspondent. At Oyingbo Market, Ebute Metta, our correspondent also observed insecticides and rat poisons being displayed in the same market spaces as dried fish, stockfish and other food ingredients. One of the traders explained that he operated from the space allocated to him by the market. Asked whether market officials were aware of the products he sold alongside food items, he said, “They are aware. They pass here regularly and come to collect money from me.” Products without visible registration details At Agboju Market, Old Ojo, Lagos, our correspondent observed other 100ml insecticide products, including Sweeper, Rocket, Ara Force and Stripe. The products did not bear visible NAFDAC registration numbers on their packaging. Their regulatory status and chemical composition could not be independently established during the investigation. One of the products, labelled Sweeper, carried a manufacturing date of August 8, 2024, and bore the name of a manufacturing business on its packaging. However, its registration status and the manufacturer’s authorisation could not be independently confirmed. The product’s appearance and smell were similar to those of some other insecticide brands observed during the investigation. However, no laboratory analysis was conducted to establish whether their chemical compositions were identical. A trader at the market described the products as alternatives to established insecticide brands, including Sniper, DD Force, Attacke and Gladiator. He claimed that they were effective. At the Timber and Building Material Market in Maza-Maza, beside the Young Shall Grow Motor Park, Lagos, our correspondent also observed small-sized chemical products being displayed alongside building materials. A trader selling some of the products explained that customers who purchased wood often requested chemicals to protect it against termites and other insects. “We sell some of these chemicals because people who buy wood from us usually request chemicals that they would use to protect the wood from termites and worms. I am not an agrochemical dealer. I am just doing my business,” he said. At Oshodi underbridge, our correspondent observed several small-scale traders displaying insecticides alongside household items such as padlocks, nail cutters and key holders. One of the traders said she sold Sniper, Gladiator, DD Force and other products to customers who wanted to control mosquitoes, cockroaches and bedbugs. “I do not sell to farmers. I sell to people for mosquito, cockroach and bedbug control,” she said. Banned pesticides circulating in markets – NAFDAC Confirming concerns about the continued circulation of prohibited agrochemicals, NAFDAC recently raised the alarm over the movement of banned and unregistered pesticides across Nigeria’s borders. The agency said smuggling remained a major challenge despite efforts to contain the situation, warning that the circulation of unsafe agrochemicals posed risks to public health, food safety and the environment. It stated that it had intensified surveillance and enforcement operations to address the movement of prohibited products into the Nigerian market through neighbouring countries and unauthorised distribution channels. In a statement signed by its Director-General, Prof Mojisola Adeyeye, NAFDAC expressed concern that pesticides lacking the required regulatory assessment could enter local markets through informal distribution channels. “The illegal movement of banned and unregistered pesticides across our borders poses a serious threat to public health, food safety and the environment,” Adeyeye stated. The agency disclosed that it seized banned agrochemicals valued at more than N800m across Ogun, Ondo, Osun and Oyo states in 2025 as part of efforts to curb the circulation of unsafe agricultural chemicals. It added that enforcement operations conducted in the North-West zone between September 2024 and July 2026 resulted in the interception and seizure of 2,974 cartons of paraquat-based pesticides valued at approximately N148.7m. According to the agency, the operations also led to the recovery of 120 cartons of chlorpyrifos-based pesticides worth more than N17m. NAFDAC further disclosed that recent operations in Kebbi State resulted in the interception of 5,619 cartons of paraquat-based products and 500 cartons of atrazine-based products. The agency said it had sealed four unauthorised pesticide and agrochemical manufacturing facilities in Bichi, Kano State, while strengthening collaboration with security and law enforcement authorities to address illegal supply networks. “Our enforcement operations are aimed at dismantling illegal supply chains, preventing prohibited products from reaching the Nigerian market, and ensuring that offenders are brought to justice,” NAFDAC said. It noted that the bans on paraquat, chlorpyrifos and atrazine took effect on January 1, 2024, November 1, 2024, and January 1, 2025, respectively, with the applicable phase-out grace periods concluding on January 1, 2026. Additionally, NAFDAC prohibited the importation, manufacture and open-market or supermarket sale of 100ml pack sizes of dichlorvos, popularly known as DDVP, due to concerns about its misuse on consumable agricultural produce. While emphasising the importance of approved pesticides to agricultural productivity, NAFDAC stressed that their handling must comply with regulatory standards to protect consumers, farmers and ecosystems. “Farmers and other pesticide users must strictly follow approved label instructions, observe recommended pre-harvest intervals, and ensure the safe disposal of empty containers to protect consumers and the environment,” the agency cautioned. The agency also disclosed that it had trained more than 2,000 agro-input dealers nationwide to promote chemical authenticity and encourage responsible pesticide management. It called on manufacturers, importers, distributors, farmers and members of the public to support regulatory enforcement by complying with statutory guidelines and reporting suspected illegal or unsafe products through its offices or official reporting channels. ‘Monitor compliance’ A Professor of Agrochemistry at the Federal University of Agriculture, Makurdi, Benue State, Lami Nnamonu, said the rejection of some agricultural products from Nigeria in Europe and other countries had been linked to the improper use of chemicals by farmers. Nnamonu explained that the inappropriate use of pesticides and preservatives could be attributed partly to inadequate monitoring and enforcement of existing chemical-use regulations. She said the situation could have economic implications for the country, including losses in foreign exchange earnings. The professor noted that pesticide residues remained a concern in food safety, adding that improper application of chemicals could result in residue levels exceeding recommended limits. She said farm produce from Nigeria had been reported to contain pesticide residues above maximum residue limits in some cases, emphasising the need for greater monitoring and farmer education. “We produce a lot of yams in Benue State, and there was a franchise to export our yam to Europe and the Americas. But at the point of checking, they discovered that our yam had pesticide residues at levels higher than the MRL. “Let them implement and monitor farmers’ compliance because they are largely uneducated. All they want is improved yields, and they do not care about what people eat but just want a bumper harvest. If the regulatory bodies are there, they will make sure that the right thing is done,” she added. Chijioke Iremeka Chijioke Iremeka is a Senior Correspondent at Punch Newspapers with 19 years of professional experience. He has reported across multiple media houses in Nigeria, covering beats such as health, features, real estate, and insurance, and has received numerous journalism awards for his work.
